text: Lessons 24 through 26 covered how to build a data pipeline that should keep five hundred twelve GPUs fed — tuned settings, sharded data, sized storage. This lesson is about what to do when all of that is in place and the GPUs are still underutilized, because finding the specific bottleneck is a diagnostic skill, not a guessing game.

Five culprits show up most often, each with its own signature. Too few workers, and step time improves roughly linearly as you add more. CPU-bound preprocessing, like tokenization or decompression, pegs the node's CPU near one hundred percent while GPU utilization dips. Missing pin_memory means a slower, synchronous copy onto the GPU. Storage throughput shows up as both CPU and GPU sitting idle at once, waiting on I/O. And a batch size that's too small spends more of each step on fixed overhead than on real work.

Guessing which one applies wastes cluster time, so the PyTorch Profiler settles it with evidence. Wrapping the training loop in a profiler context and viewing the resulting trace in TensorBoard breaks every step down into data-loading wait time, compute time, and communication time — turning "GPUs feel slow" into an exact number of milliseconds spent waiting on the loader.

It's tempting to treat num_workers as a dial that only helps when turned up. It doesn't. Each node has a fixed number of CPU cores, and workers compete with each other for that same pool. Past a certain point, adding more workers increases context-switching and memory pressure faster than it increases throughput, and step time actually gets worse. The right value is found empirically, not assumed.

Diagnosing a data loader bottleneck means distinguishing starvation from a real compute or network limit, checking the common culprits, and confirming with the profiler. Next, Lesson 28: caching strategies that fix one of the most common root causes directly.
